ch12.anchor: upon each foot he bears six toes
ch12.note: The mark of the six toes is Gu Long’s invention, but the belief behind it is old and real. Chinese tradition held that a man destined to rule was born bearing an yixiang (异相), a ‘physiognomy past nature’ — a bodily sign that Heaven had set its mandate on him. The sage-king Shun and the warlord Xiang Yu were each said to have had double pupils; the founder of the Han, Liu Bang, to bear seventy-two moles; Liu Bei, ears that reached his shoulders and arms that reached his knees. To give the royal house of the Golden Roc six toes on every foot places it in that tradition: the true king can be known, in the end, only by the body he was born in.

ch12.anchor: never again born into a king's house
ch12.note: Lu Xiaofeng quotes a cry Chinese readers would know at once. When the last emperor of the Liu Song dynasty (労宋), still a boy, was forced from his throne in 479 and led off to be killed, he is said to have wept, ‘Would that, life after life, I be born no more into a king’s house.’ The words, set down in the dynastic histories, became proverbial for the peculiar wretchedness of royalty: to be born to a throne is to be born to be betrayed and murdered for it. It is the very fate the Golden Roc’s prince had fled.

ch12.anchor: no Tian Dan, no Emperor Guangwu
ch12.note: Four rulers, set two against two. Tian Dan (田单) was the general who in 279 BCE won back the all-but-conquered state of Qi with a night charge of fire-oxen; Emperor Guangwu (光武帝) restored the fallen Han dynasty in 25 CE. Both are bywords for the man who wins a lost kingdom back. Li Houzhu (李后主, Li Yu) and the Song emperor Huizong (宋徽宗) are bywords for the opposite: each a supreme artist — Li Yu the greatest of the ci poets, Huizong a master painter and calligrapher who devised his own ‘slender-gold’ hand — and each a ruler who lost his throne and died a captive. To call the prince a ‘master of the three perfections’ (poetry, calligraphy, and painting) is to rank him with the second pair, not the first: an artist born to a crown he had no wish to fight for.

ch12.anchor: Love, from of old, leaves only regret behind
ch12.note: Lu Xiaofeng’s line turns on a pun the English can only gesture at. The dead man is named Liu Yuhen (柳余恨), and yuhen (余恨) means exactly this: ‘the regret that is left over.’ The words are the first half of a proverbial couplet — Those of deep feeling, from of old, are left with nothing but regret; the fairest dream has ever been the easiest to wake from — so that in naming the man’s fault Lu Xiaofeng speaks his name as well.

Lu Ban (鲁班), also called Gongshu Ban, was a master carpenter and engineer of the state of Lu in the fifth century BCE, credited by legend with the saw, the carpenter’s square, and every manner of ingenious device and siege-engine; he is the patron of builders and craftsmen to this day. To be named his heir, and the first hand under heaven at hidden contrivances, is to be named the one man who could unmake a maze-tower such as Huo Xiu’s — which is why Zhu Ting’s presence is the move Lu Xiaofeng has kept in reserve.

ch12.anchor: inviting the ruler into the urn
ch12.note: ‘Inviting the ruler into the urn’ (请君入瓶) is a set phrase for turning a man’s own cruelty back upon him. Under the Empress Wu of the Tang, the torturer Lai Junchen, meaning to break a fellow official, Zhou Xing, first asked him over a friendly meal how a stubborn prisoner might be made to confess. Seal him in a great jar, said Zhou Xing, and heat it with fire until he talks. Lai had such a jar brought and the fire kindled, then said: ‘A charge has come against you, elder brother; so please, step into the urn.’ Huo Xiu’s cage, built for Lu Xiaofeng, has closed on Huo Xiu himself.
